title: Origen reading
hook: a scholar and teacher of the young who read scripture on more than one level: body, soul and spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tertullian's dare, and your line was seed, not end. What looked buried or lost, and did you say the line? Day seven hundred sixty-three.

A teenage boy in Alexandria wants to run out and die beside his father, who has been arrested as a Christian. His mother can't talk him out of it. So, the story goes, she hides all his clothes, and he has to stay home. That's how the church historian Eusebius tells the beginning of Origen's life. The boy writes his father a letter instead, urging him to hold firm. His father is killed. The family is left with nothing. And the boy who couldn't leave the house becomes a teacher, and a reader of the Bible people are still learning from and arguing with. While he's still young, Eusebius says, he's put in charge of teaching people preparing for baptism. Today: how Origen read.

Origen's big idea is that scripture is built like a person. A human being, he says, has a body, a soul and a spirit. So does the Bible. The body is the plain story, the words as they stand, and he says that alone helps simpler readers. The soul is what the text says to how you live: your choices, your habits, your heart. The spirit is what it shows about God and Christ and the life to come. Not every reader is ready for every level, he says, and that's fine. A body is still a body. Then Origen makes a bolder move. Sometimes, he says, the text puts a stumbling block in the plain story on purpose, something that can't work if you take it flatly, to make you stop and look deeper. His example: Genesis counts a first day, a second, a third, with evening and morning, before it mentions the sun and moon. How can there be days with no sun? For Origen, the puzzle is a door, not a mistake. Here's where to be fair. Christians still differ on how to read a passage like that. Some read Genesis closely as history. Some read it as Origen did. Others hold the plain story and the deeper meaning together. And some of Origen's other ideas were later disputed, so churches still differ on how to remember him. But his habit of reading still echoes. Whenever a preacher says this story is about Israel and also about you, they're doing something Origen spent his life on. Take your time with a verse. Ask what it says. Then ask what it says to you. Then ask what it says about God.

Here's the practice: read one verse three ways. Settle, and breathe. Here's a short one from the Psalms, in the King James Bible: "Be still, and know that I am God." First, its body: what is it simply saying? Stop moving, and know. Then its soul: what does it say to the way you're living today? Where are you not still? Then its spirit: what does it say about God, if you're someone who asks that? Take each level slowly, one at a time. If you pray, let the verse be the prayer. If you don't, let it be a sentence you turn over in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Origen reading. A way of reading scripture on three levels, like a person: body, soul and spirit. The plain story, the life, and God.

Your line: read deeper. This week we met a letter, a Sunday, two sisters, a living human being, a fish, a seed, and now a reader. Pick one, and read it again today, slower. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Some Christians read scripture both for its plain meaning and for what it says to their lives and about God; monastic communities and some prayer groups practice slow, layered reading of a short passage, called lectio divina.
